questions.prompt: How does Ousterhout characterise complexity in software design?

options.text: Anything related to the structure of a system that makes it hard to understand and modify
The total number of lines of code in the system
The count of external libraries a system depends on
The time taken to compile the system

questions.explanation: Complexity is anything related to the structure of a software system that makes it hard to understand and modify it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are listed as symptoms of complexity?
questions.explanation: The three symptoms of complexity are change amplification, cognitive load, and unknown unknowns.

questions.prompt: According to the 'deep modules' principle, modules should have a simple interface and a comparatively more complex implementation.
questions.explanation: Modules should be deep: the interface (a cost) should be simple while the implementation (a benefit) is ideally much more complex.

questions.prompt: What is 'information leakage' in module design?

options.text: When a design decision is reflected in multiple modules, creating dependencies
When sensitive user data is exposed over the network
When comments reveal too much about the implementation
When a module logs its internal state

questions.explanation: Information leakage occurs when a design decision is reflected in multiple modules, which creates dependencies; the wider the interface the more info is leaked.

questions.prompt: Which mindset focuses on the long-term structure of the system rather than just making code work as soon as possible?
questions.explanation: Strategic programming invests time in improving the design for the long-term structure; tactical programming focuses on working code as soon as possible.

questions.prompt: One strategy for handling errors is to 'define errors out of existence' by redefining a method's behaviour so no error is required.
questions.explanation: Defining errors out of existence means redefining behaviour so that no error condition arises, e.g. avoiding unnecessary exceptions like substring's IndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.prompt: Which of these are dependency dimensions discussed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Four dependency dimensions are presented: structural, runtime/distribution, data-level, and behavioral.

questions.prompt: According to Gall's Law, a complex system that works...

options.text: Is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked
Must always be designed completely from scratch
Is always simpler than it appears

questions.explanation: Gall's Law: a complex system that works has invariably evolved from a simple system that worked; one designed from scratch never works.
